issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot reassess concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal when the issue decided by the lower courts is essentially factual.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a suit challenging a trust deed as fictitious and seeking to have the properties sold to satisfy their decree.
The two courts below found that the dedication was effective, title had passed to the deity, and the plaintiffs had failed to prove that the trust deed was fictitious.
The High Court re-examined the oral and documentary evidence and reversed those concurrent findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to reverse the concurrent factual findings in second appeal; its judgment was set aside and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under the law governing second appeals, a High Court cannot go into questions of fact, even if it considers the lower courts’ findings erroneous. Whether a trust deed was fictitious was essentially a question of fact; a finding of fact, including an inference from other facts, is not a question of law except in specified cases. The Court referred to Meenakshi Mills, Madurai v. The Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras, [1956] S.C.R. 691, and the settled line of Privy Council and Supreme Court decisions.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter before the High Court was a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The courts below reached the same findings on the relevant facts.
predicates.issue_is_essentially_factual: The issue for decision depended on whether a transaction was fictitious, a matter essentially of fact.

issues.definition: When a second appeal presents an essentially factual issue on which the courts below made concurrent findings, the High Court cannot reassess those findings.

issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff challenging a formally executed and registered document as fictitious, while also seeking to set aside an execution-court order allowing a third party’s claim to the property, bears a heavy burden of proof.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sued under Order 21, rule 63, seeking a declaration that the trust deed was sham and fictitious and that the properties could be sold to satisfy their decree.
The deed had been solemnly executed and registered.
The executing court had, after inquiry, upheld the deity’s claim to the properties under Order 21, rule 60.
The two courts below found that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their case.
issues.conclusion: The burden rested heavily on the plaintiffs to prove both that the deed was fictitious and that the executing court’s order was erroneous; the High Court misplaced that burden. The suit therefore remained dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 21, rules 60 and 63 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a plaintiff seeking to displace an execution-court order upholding a third party’s claim must affirmatively show that the order was erroneous. In a suit alleging that a solemnly executed and registered document is fictitious, the burden of proof lies heavily on the plaintiff; it becomes doubly heavy when the plaintiff also seeks to set aside such an execution-court order.

predicates.claim_suit_challenging_execution_order: The plaintiff brought a suit to challenge an order made in execution proceedings concerning a claim to property.
predicates.plaintiff_alleges_formally_executed_docu: The plaintiff alleged that a formally executed and registered document was fictitious.
predicates.order_upholds_third_party_property_claim: The execution court upheld a third party’s claim that the property belonged to that party rather than to the judgment debtor.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff brings a claim suit challenging an order that upholds a third party’s property claim and alleges that a formally executed document is fictitious, the plaintiff must prove both the alleged fiction and the error in the order.
